summary: Dynamic programme over a recursive corner-square layout: put a square of side p in a corner and fill it recursively with n1 squares, then fill the L-shaped remainder with rows of squares of side 1-p. The best p and n1 are chosen for each n, and leftover squares get side 0. Sides are shrunk by 1e-9 t

Guillotine-style row packing: rows of equal squares, using a few distinct per-row counts plus a partial last row, picked by exhaustive search over the row structure. This beats the plain k×k grid when n is not a perfect square, and leftover squares get side 0.

Recursive grid packing by dynamic programming: a unit square is split into a k×k grid (k ≤ 10), with each cell holding a scaled copy of the best packing for some number of squares. A knapsack over cells picks how many squares go in each cell, and leftover squares get side 0.

Dynamic programming over guillotine partitions of a K×K integer grid. Each rectangle holds at most c squares, with a single square of side min(w,h) as the base case, and I take the best K within a time budget and pad with zero-side squares. Dynamic programme over nested constructions. A scaled sub-square sits in a corner and an L-shaped strip of q or q−1 equal squares of side 1/q fills the rest, with a plain grid as the base case. Side lengths are shrunk by a tiny factor so touching squares keep disjoint interiors.

Axis-aligned layout found by a guillotine-cut dynamic programme on an M×M integer grid. The DP picks at most n squares with integer sides, maximising their total side, and I take the best grid resolution and rebuild its layout. Unused squares get side 0. It always includes a plain grid as a fallback

Hierarchical grid DP: split a square into a k×k grid of equal cells, distribute the n squares among the cells, and recurse. Best values come from max-plus knapsack with exponentiation by squaring; the layout is rebuilt by backtracking. Unused squares have side 0.

Tile a K×K integer grid with a few larger squares (one or two sizes, greedy placed) and unit cells, drop cells when over n, and choose K and the sizes by exhaustive search on the total side length. The remaining squares are zero-size.

Choose a k×k grid and merge aligned a×a blocks into single larger squares (merging reduces the square count with small loss), drop the cheapest unit cells if needed, and search over k, a and the number of merged blocks for the best sum for each n.

Use an m×m grid of equal squares (m about √n) and cut the square count to n by merging 2×2 or 3×3 blocks into one larger square, removing cells only for the leftover excess. The program tries several m and block mixes and keeps the best sum.

Recursive DP: each square is split into a k×k grid (k up to 4), optionally merging a j×j corner block into one big square. Sub-squares get counts by a knapsack and are refined recursively, and simple large-k grids are also considered. The result is reconstructed for any n, with leftover squares set

Take a k×k grid and merge some aligned j×j blocks into single larger squares, which cuts the square count for a small loss in total side length. A knapsack DP picks the cheapest merges to reach exactly n squares, a first-fit check confirms the blocks pack, and any shortfall is padded with zero-size

Recursive grid-subdivision: for each n, use an m×m grid and give each cell 0, 1 or several squares, with several squares filled recursively inside the cell. A knapsack DP picks the per-cell counts to maximise the sum of sides, with memoised values and padding by zero-size squares.

Axis-aligned construction. For each grid size m, take an m×m grid of side 1/m squares, merge t of the 2×2 blocks into larger squares and drop the remaining excess cells as size-0 squares, so the total count is at most n. The program tries each m and t and keeps the layout with the largest side sum.

Treat the problem as tilings by axis-aligned squares. A DP computes f(c), the best sum of sides for c squares in a unit cell. Exact dynamic programme over recursive axis-aligned layouts. Each square is either a single square or an m×m grid whose cells receive optimally split sub-counts, optionally with one merged b×b corner block. Layouts are rebuilt by backtracking. For large n the top level is a grid knapsack over cells
